entry.title: Three odd Gaussian primes conjecture for the first quadrant
entry.statement: Let $A=\{z\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\mid\operatorname{Re}(z)>0\text{ and }\operatorname{Im}(z)>0\}$, and let $K_\pi=\{z\in\pi_{\mathbb{Z}[i]}\mid\operatorname{Re}(z)\geq0\text{ and }\operatorname{Im}(z)\geq0\}$. **Three odd Gaussian primes conjecture.** For every $z\in A$ with $\max(\operatorname{Re}(z),\operatorname{Im}(z))\geq7$, the Gaussian integer $z$ is a sum of at most three odd primes from $K_\pi$. This is motivated by computational experiments on representations of Gaussian integers; the source gives no proof or resolution.

entry.title: Harmse–Remmel conjecture on c-Wilf and strong c-Wilf equivalence
entry.statement_literal:
Let $P,Q
\in\mathcal F_{n,k}$, where $
\mathcal F_{n,k}$ denotes the relevant family of generalized Euler permutations. They are **c-Wilf equivalent** when $A_P(0,t)=A_Q(0,t)$, and **strongly c-Wilf equivalent** when $A_P(x,t)=A_Q(x,t)$, where

$$
A_P(x,t)=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{t^n}{(kn)!}\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_{n,k}}x^{P\text{-mch}(F)}.
$$

**Harmse–Remmel conjecture.** $P$ and $Q$ are c-Wilf equivalent if and only if they are strongly c-Wilf equivalent. The conjecture extends Nakamura's $k=1$ formulation to $k\geq2$; the source does not state whether it has been resolved.

entry.mathematical_attempt_and_precise_gap: Strong implies avoidance by x=0; converse requires recovering every occurrence-count coefficient from all avoidance counts. Finite agreement of avoidance series cannot prove c-Wilf equivalence. A counterexample needs exact all-length avoidance identity plus one differing occurrence count; no such identity found. Nonoverlapping ordinary-permutation theorems do not automatically settle generalized Euler arrays.
